lead: Avionics is aircraft electronics, but the word covers different design goals. A civil airliner needs safety, regularity and certification. A fighter needs mission computing, survivability and weapons control. A spacecraft needs autonomy, telemetry and fault recovery far from repair. A UAV needs small size, low weight and a datalink to a remote pilot. The same building blocks recur: sensors, processing, displays, data buses, power and cooling. Their balance changes with the platform. This chapter compares the four families and shows why one avionics template cannot serve all.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 flight control basics help but are not required; Section 4.2 sets the architecture vocabulary.

sections.h3: From separate boxes to integrated avionics

blocks.text: Early aircraft carried separate radios, a gyro horizon, an altimeter and an airspeed indicator. Each box had its own wire, power and case. Integration began when digital computers could combine air data, attitude and navigation. The cockpit became fewer glass displays fed by shared computers; displays and data buses are covered in 4.2 and 4.3. A useful framework is six layers: sensors, processing, displays, data buses, power and cooling. Sensors include air data probes, inertial units, radar and electro-optical turrets. Processing turns measurements into flight guidance, mission tracks or telemetry frames. Displays present state to a crew or remote pilot. Data buses carry words with timing and error checks, such as ARINC 429 and MIL-STD-1553B (4.7). Power and cooling set what can run. Civil avionics adds certification: a failure must be shown to be extremely improbable if its effect is catastrophic. ADS-B Out is a civil example: the aircraft broadcasts position and identity at 1090 MHz for surveillance; signal details are in Unit 5. Military and spacecraft systems reuse the same layers but change the priorities.

Civil avionics optimises safety, regularity and cost. The environment is a pressurised cabin, repeated take-off and landing, lightning and icing. Redundancy is formal: duplicate or triple channels, cross-checks and dispatch rules. Certification follows failure consequence; software assurance is tied to the effect of a failure (4.9). A B737 broadcasting ADS-B Out at 1090 MHz is civil surveillance; it helps controllers see the aircraft, but it is not a navigation sensor (Unit 5).

Military avionics optimises mission success and survivability. The environment adds vibration, high g, radar illumination and electromagnetic jamming. Redundancy may be battle damage tolerance and graceful degradation, not only dispatch. Mission computing fuses radar, EO/IR, SIGINT, communications and stores management. Stores management controls weapons release; it is not a sensor. Electronic warfare (EW) detects, locates or counters threats. HUD and helmet-mounted displays keep symbols in the pilot's line of sight (4.5). MIL-STD-1553B is a common military bus. Certification is by military airworthiness and mission requirements, not civil passenger rules. The payload list matters: radar, EO/IR, SIGINT, communications, stores and science packages each need power, cooling and data paths, but sensor physics is outside this chapter.

Spacecraft avionics optimises autonomy and telemetry. A satellite cannot be repaired; it must survive launch vibration, vacuum, thermal cycling and radiation. Processing must detect faults and recover, often with redundant computers and watchdogs. Guidance computes attitude and orbit corrections; a 3-axis satellite uses reaction wheels or thrusters to hold attitude. Telemetry packs housekeeping and science data into frames; the ground segment may see the spacecraft only in short passes. Power is solar arrays plus batteries; cooling is by radiation, not air. Redundancy is sparing and fault recovery, not a quick return to a gate.

UAV avionics optimises size, weight and power. A 25 kg UAV may carry an autopilot, GNSS/INS, a datalink and a small EO/IR payload. Waypoint following is run by the autopilot; the remote pilot sends commands over a datalink. Datalink loss changes design: the UAV must loiter, return or land by itself. Redundancy is limited by mass and cost, so the design uses careful failure modes and geofencing. Treating UAV avionics as small civil avionics is a trap: limited weight, power and datalink loss change the architecture. Payloads range from EO/IR and communications to radar and SIGINT; each adds power and cooling load. See 4.8 for high-bandwidth links and 4.10 for sensors.

examples.question: Classify four avionics functions and state the numerical data: (a) ADS-B Out at 1090 MHz on a B737, (b) stores management on a fighter, (c) attitude control on a 3-axis satellite, (d) waypoint following on a 25 kg UAV.
steps: Read the platform and the primary goal. Civil values safety and regularity; military values mission and survivability; spacecraft values autonomy and telemetry; UAV values weight, power and remote control.
(a) The B737 is a civil airliner. ADS-B Out is civil surveillance, and its stated frequency is 1090 MHz.
(b) A fighter is military. Stores management controls weapons release, so it is military mission avionics.
(c) A satellite is spacecraft. Attitude control is spacecraft guidance and control; the stated axis count is 3.
(d) A 25 kg UAV is an unmanned aircraft. Waypoint following is an autopilot function; the stated mass is 25 kg.
Count the functions: four. The answer keeps the platform labels and the stated numbers: 1090 MHz, 25 kg, 3 axes and 4 functions.
examples.answer: The four functions are (a) civil, (b) military, (c) spacecraft and (d) UAV, with ADS-B Out at 1090 MHz, a 25 kg UAV and a 3-axis satellite.
examples.check:
adsb_mhz = 1090
uav_mass_kg = 25
satellite_axes = 3
functions = 4
for value in (adsb_mhz, uav_mass_kg, satellite_axes, functions):
    print(value)

traps: Treating UAV avionics as small civil avionics. Limited weight, limited power and datalink loss change the design; a UAV may need autonomous return or landing.
Calling ADS-B a navigation system. ADS-B is surveillance; it broadcasts position and identity, while navigation sensors and signal details belong to Unit 5.
Mixing payloads with sensors. Radar, EO/IR and SIGINT are sensor payloads; stores management is weapons control; communications is a link, not a sensor.

Using one certification rule for all platforms. Civil software assurance follows failure consequence, military follows airworthiness and mission needs, and spacecraft adds radiation and fault recovery.

quiz.a: Air data measurement and cockpit displays are two civil functions. Navigation and surveillance are others.

quiz.q: What does ADS-B Out broadcast, and at what frequency in the example?
quiz.a: ADS-B Out broadcasts position and identity for surveillance; the example uses 1090 MHz.

quiz.q: Why does spacecraft redundancy differ from civil aircraft redundancy?
quiz.a: A spacecraft cannot be repaired in flight and may be seen only in short ground passes. It needs fault detection, isolation and recovery, radiation tolerance and sparing, not a quick return to a gate.

quiz.q: Why is stores management classified as military avionics?
quiz.a: Stores management controls weapons release on a military platform. Its purpose is mission and weapons control, not civil passenger safety and regularity.

quiz.q: A 25 kg UAV follows waypoints after launch. Name the platform family and the avionics function.
quiz.a: Platform family: UAV. Function: waypoint following is an autopilot function, using GNSS/INS and a datalink for remote commands.

quiz.q: A UAV loses its command datalink. State two design features that reduce risk.
quiz.a: The autopilot can enter a lost-link mode such as loiter, return-to-home or automatic landing. A geofence can keep the UAV inside a safe area. Both are defined before flight.

quiz.q: Explain why 'UAV avionics is small civil avionics' is a poor design rule. Use weight, power and datalink loss.
quiz.a: A UAV has tight mass and power budgets, so it cannot carry the same redundancy and cooling as a civil airliner. It also depends on a datalink that can fail, so it needs autonomous lost-link behaviour. The architecture must trade capability for size, weight and power.

quiz.q: Compare the main certification driver for civil aircraft and for spacecraft avionics.
quiz.a: Civil certification is driven by the consequence of failure for passengers and the public; software assurance follows that consequence. Spacecraft certification is driven by mission assurance in a harsh environment: launch loads, vacuum, thermal cycling, radiation and limited repair. Both need evidence, but the hazards and recovery options differ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern civil aircraft move toward integrated modular avionics and open architectures, while military systems add open mission systems and rapid software updates. Spacecraft increasingly use autonomous fault detection, isolation and recovery, and UAVs move toward detect-and-avoid and certified cargo operations. Search terms: integrated modular avionics, open mission systems, FDIR, detect-and-avoid and ADS-B In.
